lesson.6_1.title: Risk, return and diversification
lesson.6_1.gut.prompt: You have ₹6,000 and three pretend years. Put it all in shares, in a mix, or all in savings?
lesson.6_1.gut.bridge: Higher possible reward comes with higher risk. Let's name the parts.
lesson.6_1.gut.a.label: All in shares
lesson.6_1.gut.a.result: Shares moved the most. In the pretend crash year, ₹6,000 in shares fell to ₹4,500.
lesson.6_1.gut.b.label: A mix
lesson.6_1.gut.b.result: The mix moved less. When one part fell, another part held.
lesson.6_1.gut.c.label: All in savings
lesson.6_1.gut.c.result: Savings barely moved, and grew the least.
lesson.6_1.c1.text: Every place you can keep money trades some safety for some possible growth.
lesson.6_1.c2.text: Return is what your money earns. Risk is the chance it earns less than you hoped, or loses value.
lesson.6_1.c3.text: Volatility is how sharply a price jumps up and down.
lesson.6_1.c4.text: Equity means owning a piece of a business. Debt means lending money and earning interest.
lesson.6_1.c4.sort.bond: Lending to a company for interest
lesson.6_1.c4.sort.feedback: Owners share in the ups and downs. Lenders are promised interest.
lesson.6_1.c5.text: Diversification means spreading money across different kinds of asset, so that one fall cannot sink everything. Each kind is called an asset class.
lesson.6_1.c6.text: Feelings are part of risk: selling in a panic, following the crowd, or holding on only because you have already paid.
lesson.6_1.c7.text: You will hear about fast trading in futures and options, and about crypto. Money can be lost in them very quickly. This game does not teach how to trade them.
lesson.6_1.q1.right: Yes. It limits how much any single fall can hurt.
lesson.6_1.q1.wrong: Diversification does not remove risk or promise profit. It stops one fall from sinking everything.
lesson.6_1.q1.o2: It spreads money so one fall cannot sink everything
lesson.6_1.q2.prompt: A higher possible return usually comes with higher risk.
lesson.6_1.q2.right: Correct. The chance of more comes with the chance of less.
lesson.6_1.q2.wrong: It's true. If something offers more, ask what could go wrong: the two travel together.
lesson.6_1.q3.right: Right. A share is a piece of ownership.
lesson.6_1.q3.wrong: Equity is ownership. A share makes you a part-owner; the other two are money you lend to a bank.
lesson.6_1.effect: You pick a mix and preview it under three pretend markets: Steady, Bumpy and Crash year. A preview changes nothing in your portfolio.
lesson.6_2.title: Gold and other stores of value
lesson.6_2.gut.prompt: You want ₹3,000 of gold. A coin from a jeweller has an 8% making charge. Regulated paper gold has a 0.5% cost. Which?
lesson.6_2.gut.bridge: Same metal, different costs. Here is what to look for.
lesson.6_2.gut.a.label: The coin
lesson.6_2.gut.a.result: Your ₹3,000 holds gold worth ₹2,760 on day one. You can hold it in your hand, and you must keep it safe.
lesson.6_2.gut.b.label: Paper gold
lesson.6_2.gut.b.result: Your ₹3,000 holds gold worth ₹2,985 on day one. It sits in an account, not in your hand.
lesson.6_2.c1.text: Gold is one of the oldest ways families store value.
lesson.6_2.c2.text: Physical gold comes with making charges: the jeweller's fee for crafting it. You do not get that fee back when you sell.
lesson.6_2.c3.text: A hallmark is the stamp that certifies purity. Storing the gold safely is your job.
lesson.6_2.c4.text: A gold ETF or a gold mutual fund holds gold on your behalf. It is regulated, costs less to buy and can be sold quickly.
lesson.6_2.c5.text: The costs show up on day one.
lesson.6_2.c5.reveal.prompt: ₹3,000 with an 8% making charge, and ₹3,000 with a 0.5% cost?
lesson.6_2.c6.text: Gold pays no interest. Its price rises in some years and falls in others. Property stores value too, but it is large and slow to sell. That is called illiquid.
lesson.6_2.c7.text: Before you buy gold through any app, find out who regulates it.
lesson.6_2.q1.right: Yes. It is paid when you buy and is gone when you sell.
lesson.6_2.q1.wrong: A making charge is the jeweller's fee for the work. When you sell, you are paid for the gold only.
lesson.6_2.q1.o2: The jeweller's fee for crafting, which you do not get back
lesson.6_2.q1.o3: The price of the gold itself
lesson.6_2.q2.prompt: Gold pays you interest every year.
lesson.6_2.q2.right: Correct, it's false. Gold only gains or loses value as its price moves.
lesson.6_2.q2.wrong: It's false. Gold pays nothing while you hold it. Any gain comes only from a higher price.
lesson.6_2.q3.prompt: ₹3,000 of jewellery with an 8% making charge holds how much gold value?
lesson.6_2.q3.right: Right: 8% of ₹3,000 is ₹240, so ₹2,760 of gold is left.
lesson.6_2.effect: Your Gold bucket opens. You choose between physical gold and regulated paper gold, with the cost of each shown.
lesson.6_3.title: Mutual funds and SIP
lesson.6_3.gut.prompt: You start a monthly SIP. Two months later the market falls 20%. What do you do?
lesson.6_3.gut.bridge: Nobody knows what markets will do next. Here is how the tools work.
lesson.6_3.gut.a.label: Sell everything
lesson.6_3.gut.a.result: You get back less than you put in. The fall is now a real loss.
lesson.6_3.gut.b.label: Hold, and keep the SIP going
lesson.6_3.gut.b.result: Your monthly amount now buys more units at the lower price.
lesson.6_3.gut.c.label: Hold, but pause the SIP
lesson.6_3.gut.c.result: You keep what you have, and stop buying while prices are low.
lesson.6_3.c1.text: A mutual fund pools money from many people. A manager uses it to buy a basket of shares or bonds. The company that runs the fund is called an AMC.
lesson.6_3.c2.text: You own units of the fund. The price of one unit is the NAV, and it changes every day.
lesson.6_3.c3.text: A SIP puts in a fixed amount every month. A lumpsum puts in one amount at once.
lesson.6_3.c4.text: When prices fall, the same SIP amount buys more units. When prices rise, it buys fewer. This is rupee-cost averaging.
lesson.6_3.c5.text: An index fund copies a list of companies and charges less. An actively managed fund tries to beat the list and charges more. Neither is guaranteed to win.
lesson.6_3.c6.text: The yearly fee is the expense ratio. Regular plans include a distributor's commission. Direct plans do not. The fee difference compounds.
lesson.6_3.c6.reveal.prompt: ₹5,000 a month for 20 years at an assumed 12% a year, against 11%. This is an assumption, not a promise.
lesson.6_3.c6.reveal.answer: About ₹49.96 lakh against ₹43.68 lakh. One point of yearly return is about ₹6.28 lakh.
lesson.6_3.c7.text: Mutual funds are regulated by SEBI. Returns are never guaranteed and can be negative.
lesson.6_3.c7.reveal.prompt: ₹500 a month at an assumed 12% a year. This is an assumption, not a promise.
lesson.6_3.c7.reveal.answer: 10 years: about ₹1.16 lakh, with ₹60,000 put in. 20 years: about ₹5 lakh. 30 years: about ₹17.65 lakh.
lesson.6_3.q1.right: Yes. A SIP is a fixed amount, invested every month.
lesson.6_3.q1.wrong: A SIP is a monthly habit: the same amount goes in every month. It guarantees nothing.
lesson.6_3.q1.o1: Puts in one large amount once
lesson.6_3.q1.o2: Puts in a fixed amount every month
lesson.6_3.q2.prompt: Prices fall. What does your fixed SIP amount buy this month?
lesson.6_3.q2.right: Right. The same rupees buy more units when each unit is cheaper.
lesson.6_3.q2.wrong: When the price of a unit falls, the same rupees buy more units. That is rupee-cost averaging.
lesson.6_3.q3.prompt: A mutual fund's past return is a promise of its future return.
lesson.6_3.q3.right: Correct, it's false. Past returns are history. Future returns are unknown and can be negative.
lesson.6_3.q3.wrong: It's false. No one can promise a market return. Past years only show what already happened.
lesson.6_3.effect: Your SIP / Mutual fund bucket opens. You choose a monthly SIP in multiples of ₹100, or none.
lesson.6_4.title: Shares and the stock market
lesson.6_4.gut.prompt: A message says one company's stock "will double in a month". What do you do?
lesson.6_4.gut.bridge: Shares can be part of a plan. Tips are not a plan.
lesson.6_4.gut.a.label: Put in ₹2,000
lesson.6_4.gut.a.result: In our pretend market the stock jumps 15%, then falls 40%. Your ₹2,000 becomes about ₹1,380.
lesson.6_4.gut.b.label: Ignore it
lesson.6_4.gut.b.result: Your money stays where it was.
lesson.6_4.gut.c.label: Check who sent it
lesson.6_4.gut.c.result: The sender is not registered to give investment advice. You leave it alone.
lesson.6_4.c1.text: When you buy a share, you own a small piece of a company.
lesson.6_4.c2.text: Shares are bought and sold on a stock exchange. Sensex and Nifty are scoreboards that track groups of large companies.
lesson.6_4.c3.text: Shares are held electronically in a demat account.
lesson.6_4.c4.text: Prices move with news, profits and mood. A company may also pay out part of its profit as a dividend.
lesson.6_4.c4.reveal.prompt: Does a rising price mean the company itself improved?
lesson.6_4.c4.reveal.answer: Not always. Price is what people pay today. Value is what the business is worth. The two can drift apart.
lesson.6_4.c5.text: A tip is not research. The person spreading it may profit when you buy.
lesson.6_4.c6.text: Share prices can stay low for years. Money you will need soon sits badly in something that swings.
lesson.6_4.q1.right: Yes. A share makes you a part-owner.
lesson.6_4.q1.wrong: A share is ownership. You share in the company's ups and downs.
lesson.6_4.q1.o2: A small piece of ownership in a company
lesson.6_4.q2.prompt: If many people in a group chat are buying a stock, it is safe to buy.
lesson.6_4.q2.right: Correct, it's false. A crowd is not a reason. Some tips are spread so that others can sell to you.
lesson.6_4.q2.wrong: It's false. Many buyers do not make a stock safe, and some tips are pushed on purpose.
lesson.6_4.q3.prompt: What do Sensex and Nifty show?
lesson.6_4.q3.right: Right. They are scoreboards for groups of large companies.
lesson.6_4.q3.wrong: Sensex and Nifty track groups of large companies. They show the general direction of the market.
lesson.6_4.q3.o2: How a group of large companies' shares are doing
lesson.6_4.effect: Your Shares bucket opens. You choose how much to put in, if any.
lesson.6_5.title: How each option behaved over time
lesson.6_5.gut.prompt: You have money for a trip in 1 year, and money for something 7 years away. What changes about what can go wrong?
lesson.6_5.gut.bridge: Let's look at the same options over different stretches of time.
lesson.6_5.gut.a.label: Nothing changes
lesson.6_5.gut.a.result: Time changes a lot. A fall just before you need the money leaves no time to recover.
lesson.6_5.gut.b.label: With 1 year, a fall may not recover in time
lesson.6_5.gut.b.result: Yes. With more years there is more time to recover, though nothing is certain.
lesson.6_5.c1.text: One option can behave very differently over 1 year and over many years.
lesson.6_5.c2.text: Your time horizon is how long the money can stay untouched.
lesson.6_5.c3.text: Shares, in our Bumpy pretend market.
lesson.6_5.c3.reveal.prompt: ₹1,000 in shares after 1 year, 3 years and 5 years?
lesson.6_5.c3.reveal.answer: ₹1,220, then ₹1,161, then ₹1,405. It went up, came down, and went up again.
lesson.6_5.c4.text: A fixed deposit, in the same pretend market.
lesson.6_5.c4.reveal.prompt: ₹1,000 in a fixed deposit after 1 year, 3 years and 5 years?
lesson.6_5.c5.text: In this pretend market shares ended a little higher, and the ride was rougher. These are pretend numbers, not a forecast.
lesson.6_5.c6.text: How you split your money across kinds of asset is your asset allocation.
lesson.6_5.q1.right: Yes. It is how long you can leave the money alone.
lesson.6_5.q1.wrong: A time horizon is the time until you need the money.
lesson.6_5.q1.o2: How long the money can stay untouched
lesson.6_5.q1.o3: The date a company was started
lesson.6_5.q2.prompt: Over one year, an asset that swings a lot can end lower than it started.
lesson.6_5.q2.right: Correct. A single year can be a falling year.
lesson.6_5.q2.wrong: It's true. In our Bumpy pretend market, shares fell in the second year.
lesson.6_5.q3.right: Right. It describes the split, not any single choice.
lesson.6_5.q3.wrong: Asset allocation is the split: how much sits in each kind of asset.
lesson.6_5.q3.o2: How your money is split across kinds of asset
lesson.6_5.effect: Your allocation chart appears. It shows how your money is split across kinds of asset.
